claim: The ISS circles Earth about every 90 minutes at 5 miles per second, so its crew passes through 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every 24 hours.

beats.caption: 16 sunrises. Every day.
beats.vo: Astronauts see sixteen sunrises every single day.

beats.caption: 5 miles per second
beats.vo: The International Space Station flies at five miles per second. That is fast enough to circle the whole Earth about every ninety minutes.

beats.caption: Light, shadow, light again
beats.vo: Every lap, it slides out of daylight into Earth's shadow, and then back into the light. Each time it comes back, the sun rises.

beats.caption: 16 laps = 16 sunrises + 16 sunsets
beats.vo: Sixteen laps in twenty four hours means sixteen sunrises, and sixteen sunsets, every day.

beats.caption: ~3,000 sunrises in 6 months
beats.vo: Stay up there for six months, and you will watch close to three thousand sunrises. Would you ever get tired of one?

sources.text: NASA, International Space Station Facts and Figures: 5 miles per second, orbit about every 90 minutes, 16 orbits and 16 sunrises and sunsets in 24 hours. https://www.nasa.gov/international-space-station/space-station-facts-and-figures/
Six-month figure is simple arithmetic: 16 sunrises x about 180 days = about 2,900.
